content: Folate deficiency refers to a lack of folic acid, an essential compound required for the normal production of red blood cells. Folic acid, also known as vitamin B9 or pteroylglutamic acid, is part of the vitamin B complex. Adults are recommended to consume 400 micrograms (mcg) of folate daily. Women planning pregnancy or who may become pregnant should aim for 400 to 800 mcg of folic acid per day. The anemia associated with folate deficiency arises from impaired DNA precursor synthesis, particularly thymine synthesis, which is crucial for normal erythropoiesis and depends on products of the methionine synthase (MTR) reaction. Other cell lines, such as white blood cells and platelets, may also be reduced due to impaired division of precursor cells. Examination of the bone marrow may reveal megaloblastic hematopoiesis. Folate deficiency anemia is easily treatable with folic acid supplementation. Folate deficiency was first identified by Lucy Wills, an English hematologist, in 1931 during her research in India in the late 1920s and early 1930s on macrocytic anemia in pregnancy. There is no universally established classification system for folate deficiency. However, it can be categorized based on causative factors. In the human body, folic acid plays several critical roles, including the production and maintenance of new cells, DNA and RNA synthesis, carrying one-carbon groups for various methylation reactions, and preventing DNA changes, which helps reduce cancer risk. Common causes of folate deficiency include gastrointestinal conditions such as malabsorption syndromes and diseases that obstruct folate absorption. Oncological causes, including leukemia, stomach cancer, and liver cancer, are life-threatening and require prompt differentiation and diagnosis. Folate deficiency must be distinguished from other diseases associated with macrocytic anemia, such as vitamin B12 deficiency, alcoholic liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, and aplastic anemia. While folate deficiency can affect individuals of all ages, it is most commonly seen in preschool children, pregnant women, and older adults. Contributing factors include congenital defects, malabsorptive disorders, and alcohol abuse. Certain medications are also associated with an increased risk of folate deficiency. Routine screening for folate deficiency anemia is not typically recommended for asymptomatic patients. However, it can present with features of anemia and may lead to severe complications if left untreated. The prognosis for patients with folate deficiency is generally favorable, with clinical and hematological parameters typically reversing after eight weeks of treatment. There is no single diagnostic test or gold standard for diagnosing folate deficiency. A thorough medical history is crucial, as the signs and symptoms of folate deficiency are often subtle and nonspecific. Physical examination findings may vary; some patients appear normal, while others with moderate to severe anemia may present as pale, malnourished, or underdeveloped. Anemia can affect all organ systems. Laboratory tests used to diagnose folate deficiency include a complete blood count, peripheral smear, serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, serum indirect bilirubin levels, serum folate levels, red blood cell (RBC) folate levels, and plasma or serum homocysteine levels. Imaging studies do not typically reveal findings specific to folate deficiency. Bone marrow biopsy, though not routinely performed, may sometimes aid in diagnosis. Standard treatment involves oral folic acid supplementation at doses of 1 to 5 mg per day for one to four months or until complete hematologic recovery occurs. The oral route is effective even in cases of malabsorption. It is essential to rule out and treat vitamin B12 deficiency before administering folic acid to patients with megaloblastic anemia, as folic acid supplementation can exacerbate neurological complications of untreated vitamin B12 deficiency. There is no surgical treatment for folate deficiency. The primary source of folic acid for the body is dietary intake. Consuming foods rich in folic acid can prevent folate deficiency.
